items.title: Amor Fati: The Formula for Human Greatness
items.description: Amor fati — loving what happens rather than merely tolerating it — is the Stoic posture most directly applicable to operating in volatile environments. Holiday traces the concept from Nietzsche back to Marcus Aurelius, making the case that acceptance of circumstance is not passivity but the precondition for clear action.

items.title: No, America is not in a 'stealth manufacturing boom'
items.description: Rigorous takedown of the claim that tariffs are quietly reviving U.S. manufacturing; Smith shows the data do not support the narrative and that tariff headwinds are canceling industrial tailwinds.

items.description: Marcus Aurelius writing privately to himself about impermanence, duty, and the discipline of perception. Book II is the sharpest, most quotable entry point to the entire Meditations and the clearest framework for staying rational under pressure.

items.title: The Most Important Thing
items.description: Marks argues that second-level thinking is the only durable source of investment edge. The clearest statement of how to think about risk and price rather than risk and outcome.

items.title: The Enchiridion
items.description: The most concentrated distillation of Stoic practice ever written, built around the dichotomy of control. Functions as a hard reset for any week defined by variables outside your hands.

items.title: What if a few AI companies end up with all the money and power?
items.description: Smith thinks seriously through the Robot Lords scenario in which AI concentration produces entities with unprecedented economic and political power. The piece maps conditions under which concentration becomes irreversible and what policy interventions have realistic chance of working.

items.title: Risk Revisited
items.description: Marks dismantles the textbook definition of risk as volatility and replaces it with a far more useful framework: risk is the probability of permanent, unrecoverable loss. For anyone allocating capital in illiquid markets the distinction changes what you model and what you price.

items.title: Mustafa Suleyman: AI development won't hit a wall anytime soon ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ here's why
items.description: Mustafa Suleyman argues human intuitions about linear progress are ill-equipped to model exponential AI growth. His framework for thinking about compounding capability is applicable to anyone pricing long-duration risk. A substantive counterweight to AI fatigue narratives.

items.title: I Told You This Would End Badly
items.description: Noah Smith argues that structural warning signs of Trump's decision-making failures were visible long before the Iran war, and that ignoring expert judgment across domains has a predictable endpoint. Worth reading as a framework for recognizing how organizations discount low-probability, high-consequence warnings until they materialize.
